note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

ecclesiastical.note: The Italianate Latin of the Roman rite and of virtually all choral singing: C and G soften before e and i, V is [v], AE is simply [e], H is silent, and vowel length is gone. Almost every clip here is an Italian voice reading an Italian spelling, because the two systems very nearly coincide. Understand 'ecclesiastical' as the modern Roman standard — medieval England, Germany and France each read Latin through their own vernacular, and the Italianate form became universal in the church only under Pius X.

0.why: Church Latin a is the Italian a — a pure open [a] with no English fronting to [æ] and no reduction to schwa.
0.compromise: None. Note that this clip runs at normal speed where the classical one is slowed: ecclesiastical Latin has no long/short vowel contrast at all, and that absence is itself audible between the two buttons.

1.why: B is [b] in both systems. What moves is the vowel: the Italianate manuals give Latin e as the e of 'met', so the name is [bɛ] where the classical is a close, long [beː]. The grave accent asks Italian for exactly that open vowel.
1.compromise: If the voice flattens the written accent the vowel closes toward [e]. The consonant is unaffected either way.

2.why: The defining letter of this system. Before e and i, C is [tʃ] — Cicero is CHEE-cheh-roh, Caesar is CHAY-zar, excelsis is ehk-SHEL-sees. Italian orthography gives it for free: 'ce' is [tʃe] with no coaxing at all.
2.compromise: None. This is an Italian voice reading an Italian spelling to produce an Italianate sound — as close to simply correct as anything in this hall.

3.why: Italian d is a dental [d], which is what both systems want; only the vowel of the name moves, to the open [ɛ] of church Latin.

4.why: Italian 'è' is the open [ɛ] that the Liber Usualis and every church-Latin manual prescribe for Latin e — the vowel of English 'met', held steady, never gliding to 'ay'.
4.compromise: None. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

5.why: The two systems agree completely on this letter, so it is deliberately the same clip in both. A Spanish voice is used because Spanish lowers /e/ to [ɛ] in a closed syllable — exactly Latin short e — and takes a word-final consonant without appending a vowel, which Italian, whose words almost all end in vowels, does less reliably.
5.compromise: None of consequence in the sound. The name itself is a convention: the Roman grammarians name the continuants with a leading e (ef, el, em, en, er, es), but some ancient sources give fe instead, and usage varied.

6.why: The companion to C. Before e and i, G is [dʒ] — Regina is reh-JEE-nah, Agnus is AH-nyoos. Italian 'ge' is [dʒe] natively, so the Italian spelling is the recipe.
6.compromise: The system's other famous G rule, GN as the palatal [ɲ] of Agnus Dei, is not present in the letter's name and cannot be heard here.

7.why: H is silent in church Latin, and Italian h is silent in Italian. An Italian voice reading 'ha' therefore produces precisely what a Roman cantor produces: nothing but the vowel. The orthography does the work for us.
7.compromise: The clip is consequently indistinguishable from A. That is the honest result, not a failure of the recipe — but it is why Italians call the letter acca rather than trying to say its Latin name. Church Latin keeps exactly one exception: mihi and nihil are read MEE-kee and NEE-keel, the h hardening to [k].

8.why: Italian i is a pure [i] with no diphthongisation, which is Latin i in every system.
8.compromise: No length is marked because church Latin has none to mark. The letter's consonantal value is [j] here as in classical — Iesus is YEH-zoos — but that is not in the name and is not heard.

9.why: Italian c before a is [k]. K survives in church Latin only in the few places it survives in Latin at all, and is always [k].
9.compromise: None. Church Latin does not aspirate its stops any more than classical Latin did, so the Italian unaspirated [k] is right for both systems — an English 'kay' would be wrong for both.

10.why: Identical in both systems, so it is the same clip. Spanish 'el' is [ɛl]: the closed syllable gives the right short e, and the l is a clear alveolar [l], nothing like the dark English one.
10.compromise: None. The velarised l pinguis that the Roman grammarians describe is a classical question and does not arise here — church Latin l is clear, as Italian l is.

11.why: Identical in both systems. Spanish closed-syllable [ɛ] and a clean final [m].
11.compromise: None. Worth saying that this is a point where the systems part company in the language even though they agree in the name: church Latin does not nasalise final -m away, it pronounces it fully, as anyone who has sung Amen or Dona nobis pacem has heard.

12.why: Identical in both systems. Spanish 'en' is [ɛn], the target exactly.
12.compromise: The velar [ŋ] before c, g and q is not in the name and is not heard.

13.why: Church Latin o is the open [ɔ] of English 'for' — Italian ò exactly — as against the close, long [oː] of the classical name.
13.compromise: Depends on the voice honouring the written grave accent; if it does not, the vowel closes toward [o] and the difference from the classical clip narrows to length alone. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

14.why: Italian initial p is unaspirated, which church Latin wants as much as classical does. Only the vowel differs from the classical name.

15.why: Written cu rather than qu, because Italian qu is [kw] and the letter's NAME is a bare [ku] with no glide in it.
15.compromise: The name therefore does not demonstrate the letter's value. Qu is [kw] in church Latin as in classical — qui is kwee, requiem is REH-kwee-em — but you have to be told that; the name will not show it.

16.why: Identical in both systems, so it is the same clip: Spanish gives [ɛ] in the closed syllable and a genuine apical rhotic. No English voice available produces anything but the English approximant, which is wrong for every variety of Latin.
16.compromise: Spanish word-final r is normally a single tap [ɾ]. Church Latin r is flipped or trilled as Italian's is, so this clip is slightly under-rolled; the classical clip has the same shortfall for the same reason.

17.why: The name is [ɛs] in both systems and this is the same clip. Spanish 'es' gives the right open vowel and a firmly voiceless s.
17.compromise: Church Latin does differ from classical here — it voices s between vowels, so miserere is mee-zeh-REH-reh and Iesus is YEH-zoos — but the letter's name contains no intervocalic s, so the clip cannot show the one rule that matters.

18.why: 'Tè' is a real Italian word, so the reading is entirely safe, and it gives an unaspirated dental [t] with the open vowel church Latin wants.
18.compromise: The system's signature T rule — ti before a vowel becomes [tsi], so gratia is GRAH-tsee-ah and etiam is EH-tsee-am — is not in the name and cannot be heard here.

19.why: The sign's name is still just the vowel, [u]. Italian u is a pure back rounded vowel. It runs at normal speed where the classical clip is slowed, because church Latin has no length contrast.
19.compromise: The single largest audible difference between the two systems lives in this letter's CONSONANT and neither clip can say it, because the name has no consonant in it. Classical [w] against ecclesiastical [v]: Ave Maria is AH-veh, veni is VEH-nee — where the classical is WEH-nee. That contrast has to be read, not heard.

20.why: Italian reads x as [ks], and 'ex' is a live Italian loanword, so [ɛks] comes out cleanly. A Spanish voice would risk the colloquial reduction of ex- to [es].
20.compromise: Church Latin softens x before e and i — in excelsis Deo is een ehk-SHEL-sees — which the name does not show.

21.why: Two ecclesiastical rules land in one short phrase. AE is simply [ɛ] in church Latin, so Graeca is GREH-kah, not GRY-kah; and the phrase happens to be the living Italian name of the letter, i greca, so an Italian voice is on native ground. The grave accent pins both the stress and the open vowel.
21.compromise: The letter itself is [i] in church Latin — Kyrie is KEE-ree-eh — the Greek front rounded vowel having been abandoned entirely. So the name describes the letter's origin rather than its sound.

22.why: Italian zeta is [ˈdzɛta], which is exactly the church-Latin reading: z as the dz of English 'adze', open vowel, no length.
22.compromise: None. Italian and ecclesiastical Latin coincide here so completely that the recipe is simply the Italian word.

classical.note: Republican and Augustan Latin as reconstructed by Allen's Vox Latina and stated in this hall's own letter values: C always [k], G always [g], V as [w], AE as [ai], H a real breath, no palatalisation anywhere, p/t/k unaspirated, and vowel length phonemic. Italian supplies the unaspirated stops and the pure vowels, and its ch/gh and é/è spellings force the hard consonants and the close vowels; Spanish supplies the six consonant-final names, where its closed-syllable [ɛ] is Latin short e exactly; German supplies the one sound Italian cannot make, the [h]. Rate is the only handle on vowel length, so the long-vowel names are slowed.

0.why: Italian a is a pure open [a] in every position — the 'father' vowel the hall names — with none of the English fronting to [æ] and none of the reduction to schwa. Slowed, it reads as the long ā the letter is named with.
0.compromise: Rate is a crude stand-in for phonemic length: it slows the whole utterance rather than the vowel alone. Latin's short a is the same vowel simply cut shorter, which no rate setting can demonstrate in a single clip.

1.why: Italian b is a plain voiced [b], and the acute accent forces the close [e] that Latin long ē was, against the open [ɛ] of short e. English 'bee' would give the wrong vowel altogether.
1.compromise: If the voice ignores the written accent the vowel drifts open toward [ɛ]; the consonant is unaffected. Length is approximated by rate.

2.why: The most important clip in the hall. Classical C is always [k] — Cicero is KIH-keh-roh, Caesar is KYE-sar. Italian 'ce' would give [tʃe], the ecclesiastical value and the exact error this system exists to correct, so the digraph ch is used instead, which is [k] in Italian without exception. Italian [k] is also unaspirated, where an English 'kay' would add the puff of breath Latin did not have.
2.compromise: Vowel length is by rate only.

3.why: Italian d is a true dental [d], articulated against the teeth as Latin d was, without the alveolar retraction of English.
3.compromise: Length by rate only, and the vowel's aperture depends on the voice honouring the acute accent, as with bē.

4.why: Italian 'e', the conjunction, is a clean close [e] with no offglide: Latin long ē is English 'they' with the y taken off the end.
4.compromise: The string carries no accent, so the voice may render it nearer [ɛ] — the short value. The contrast with short e is then carried by the slowed rate alone, which is weaker than it should be. An accented 'é' risks being read as a foreign spelling; this is the safer of two imperfect options.

5.why: Spanish lowers /e/ to [ɛ] in a closed syllable, which is Latin short e exactly, and Spanish takes a word-final consonant without appending a vowel — Italian, whose words almost all end in vowels, is less reliable at that. The result is a clean [ɛf].
5.compromise: None of consequence in the sound. The name is a grammarians' convention: the continuants are named with a leading e (ef, el, em, en, er, es) in most ancient sources, but some give fe instead.

6.why: Italian 'ge' is [dʒe]; the digraph gh forces the hard [g] that Latin G always had, in every position and before every vowel. Spurius Carvilius Ruga barred the C for this sound in the third century BCE and it never softened in classical speech.

7.why: Italian h is silent in every position, so an Italian voice cannot say this letter at all — it would produce a bare [a]. German h is a clean [h] and German aa is the long [aː] of Haar and Saal, which is both the right consonant and the right vowel. An English 'hah' would give the back [ɑː] instead.
7.compromise: German gives a firmer, fully articulated [h] than a Roman used. Latin h was weakly breathed and widely dropped altogether — Catullus 84 exists to mock a man for over-aspirating it. Take this clip as the letter at its strongest, not at its usual.

8.why: Italian i is a pure [i], the vowel of 'machine', with no diphthongisation and no laxing to [ɪ].
8.compromise: Length by rate. The letter's other value — consonantal [j], so that iam is 'yam' and Iesus is 'YEH-soos' — is not in its name and is not heard here.

9.why: Italian c before a is an unaspirated [k] followed by a pure [a] — which is the whole name. English 'kay' would both aspirate the stop and diphthongise the vowel to [eɪ], getting two things wrong at once.

10.why: Spanish 'el' is [ɛl]: closed-syllable lowering gives the right short e, and the l is a clear alveolar [l], not the dark English one of 'full'.
10.compromise: Genuinely imperfect. The Roman grammarians describe a velarised l pinguis before consonants and word-finally — which is exactly the position this name puts it in. Spanish gives a clear l instead, so the true classical sound here would be somewhat closer to an English 'ell' than to what you will hear.

11.why: As el: Spanish closed-syllable [ɛ] and a clean final [m].
11.compromise: None for the name. The letter's most distinctive classical behaviour — word-final -m nasalising the vowel in front of it rather than closing as a full consonant, so that rem is close to [rẽː] — cannot be shown by a clip of the name.

12.why: Spanish 'en' is [ɛn], the target exactly, with a clean alveolar nasal.
12.compromise: The velar [ŋ] allophone before c, g and q — the ng of 'sing' in anguis and quinque — is not in the name and is not heard.

13.why: The acute forces Italian's close [o] — 'note' with the glide removed — against the open [ɔ] the bare conjunction 'o' would give, which is the short Latin value rather than the long one this name has.
13.compromise: Length is by rate, and the aperture depends on the voice honouring the accent. If it does not, you get short o's quality with long o's duration. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

14.why: Italian initial p is UNASPIRATED, and that is the entire point of this letter: the hall states 'no puff of breath'. An English voice saying 'pay' produces [pʰ] — which in the neighbouring Greek hall is the letter phi, and in Latin is not P at all.

15.why: Written cu, not qu: Italian qu is [kw], and the letter's NAME is a bare [kuː] with no glide in it. Italian c before u is an unaspirated [k], and Italian u is a pure back rounded vowel.
15.compromise: The letter's actual value — the labiovelar [kʷ] of 'quick', which is the only environment Q ever appears in — is therefore not demonstrated by its name. The name is just k plus a long u.

16.why: Spanish gives [ɛ] in the closed syllable and a genuine apical rhotic made with the tongue tip. No English voice available produces anything but the English approximant, which is not a Latin sound in any period.
16.compromise: Spanish word-final r is normally a single tap [ɾ], not a trill. Persius calls R the littera canina, the dog's letter, for the growl of a full rolled trill — and that growl is precisely what this clip does not deliver. Italian trills more reliably in this position but handles the bare string 'er' less reliably as text; neither option is clean.

17.why: Spanish 'es' is [ɛs] — the right short vowel, and an s that is always voiceless, never the [z] the hall explicitly warns against. Castilian s is additionally apico-alveolar, made with the tongue tip, which is how Latin s is generally reconstructed and which gives it a slightly hushed quality quite unlike the English s.
17.compromise: None of consequence. This is one of the more securely right clips in the hall.

18.why: Italian t is dental and unaspirated, as Latin t was, and 'té' is a real Italian word so the reading is entirely safe. An English 'tay' would aspirate to [tʰ] and diphthongise the vowel.

19.why: The classical name of this sign is simply its vowel, a long [uː] as in 'rule'. Italian u is a pure back rounded vowel with no onglide or offglide, and the slowed rate carries the length.
19.compromise: The name teaches nothing about the letter's famous consonantal value, [w] — veni, vidi, vici as weh-nee, wee-dee, wee-kee, and IVLIVS as YOO-lee-oos. No available voice says a Latin letter-name containing that sound, because the name does not contain it. The contrast with ecclesiastical [v] is the largest single difference between the two systems and neither button can play it.

20.why: Italian reads x as [ks] and 'ex' is a live Italian loanword, so [ɛks] comes out cleanly, with the open short e the name wants. A Spanish voice would risk the very common colloquial reduction of ex- to [es].

21.why: Three things at once. Italian gr is a hard [g]; the spelling ai is a true falling diphthong in Italian, which is what classical AE was — Caesar as KYE-sar, not CHAY-sar; and c before a is an unaspirated [k]. The grave accent pins the stress onto the diphthong, without which the voice would split the word as gra-i-ca and stress the i.
21.compromise: The long ī of the first word is not lengthened, because slowing would drag the whole two-word phrase. And the letter's own sound — the front rounded [y] of French u and German ü, which is exactly why Cicero's generation borrowed the character a second time — is not present in its name at all. The name says only 'the Greek i'.

22.why: Italian word-initial z in zeta is the affricate [dz], one of the two values this hall states for Latin z, and the acute accent asks for the close long ē of the Greek name it was borrowed with.
22.compromise: Genuinely uncertain, and the uncertainty is in the scholarship rather than the synthesis. Latin z is variously reconstructed as a plain [z], as [dz], and as a long [zz] between vowels; the letter existed only for Greek loanwords and was readmitted to the alphabet barely a century before Augustus. This clip commits to [dz] because Italian offers it cleanly and the hall lists it — a plain [z] would be equally defensible.
